$$

$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(1)^{3}-3(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 0 & =1-3-6+C \\ C & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the skateboarder at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-6t+8.$

To find the time interval in which the skateboarder is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-6t+8=(t-1)({t}^{2}-2t-8)<0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=12-3{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=15\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 12-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-6(2) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (12-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =12t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=15.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12(1)-(1)^{3}+C & =15 \\ 11+C & =15\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+12t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4+12(2)-(2)^{3}=20\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
questions.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=8\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ({t}^{1/3}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(8)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{3}{4}(8)^{4/3}-8+C \\ 4 & =12-8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t & =0 \\ t(\frac{3}{4}{t}^{1/3}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\frac{64}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we discard the solution $t=0.$ Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{64}{27}\,\text{s}.$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int -\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=\frac{1}{3}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{4}{(4)}+C \\ \frac{1}{3} & =1+C \\ C & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{4}{t} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ t & =\frac{12}{2} \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=6\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{4}{15}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{4}{15}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{4}{15}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}=0 \\ \frac{2}{5}{t}^{3/2}(\frac{5}{3}-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{5}{3}\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{4}{t}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-8\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary. Do not round your answer.

The particle is stationary at $t=$
{{field-1}}$\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{4}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-8.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+C \\ -8 & =0+C \\ C & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)-8.$ 

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)-8 & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =2 \\ t & ={e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t={e}^{2}\,\text{s}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,$ where $t > 0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time $t=0.$ This means $v(0) = 0,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}-6(0)+C \\ 0 & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

$$
v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.
$$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v > 0.$ This gives

$$
t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094076/assets/03b5ff6282d59038cbb355c0c3f017b544f286228ba4c3a82329897b4b43674c.png)

The particle moves to the right when $v(t)$ is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when $t>2.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2t-6$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s$, determine the moments in time when the particle is stationary.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$
